findings.title: Flags left unset override the defaults with undefined
findings.scenario: Running the CLI with no flags makes cli.js pass { baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined }. Object spread copies keys whose value is undefined, so config.retries becomes undefined. The check `0 <= undefined` is false, so the loop never runs, fetch is never called, and get() throws undefined. Even if that were fixed, the URL would come out as 'undefined/status'. This breaks the stated goal of keeping the current defaults when a flag is not given.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No tests exist (Glob **/*.{test,spec}.js found nothing). Object spread does not skip keys set to undefined.

findings.whyNotPrevented: parseArgs only checks that the value is a string. Nothing checks the number before it reaches the client.

findings.title: Lock is never released when a payout has no bank account, which stalls the worker
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: A payout with no accountNumber: acquire() holds `payout:<id>`, the check throws before the try/finally starts, and release() never runs. runPayouts catches the error and calls job.retryLater(). When that job comes back, acquire() waits forever on held.get(key).promise. The worker handles jobs one at a time with for-await, so every payout after it also stops being processed.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only release() call is in the finally block, and the new early exit is above the try. locks.js has no timeout, and the repo has no tests.

findings.title: Moving payouts.get above the try also leaks the lock when the read fails
findings.scenario: payouts.get rejects, for example on a DB timeout, or payouts.update on line 8 rejects. Before this change the get ran inside the try, so finally released the lock. Now the lock stays held, and when the job is retried it hangs forever on acquire().
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing outside the try/finally releases the lock, and no test checks that the lock is released when something fails.

findings.title: A payout that can never succeed is retried forever instead of staying failed
findings.scenario: Once the lock leak is fixed, a payout with no bank account throws PayoutError. The worker catches every error and calls retryLater, so the job keeps coming back, gets marked failed again and throws again, and is never acked. The author wanted the payout marked failed and done.
findings.whyNotPrevented: runPayouts treats every error the same way and does not check for PayoutError.

findings.title: The missing-account check runs before the already-sent check, so a sent payout can be overwritten as failed
findings.scenario: A payout with status 'sent' whose accountNumber was later cleared, for example after the account was deleted, gets re-run. It is rewritten as status 'failed', which replaces the record that the transfer succeeded.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The status === 'sent' early return now comes after the new check.

findings.title: No test covers the missing-bank-account path
findings.scenario: No test checks that the payout is marked failed, that bank.send is not called, or that the lock is released, so the lock leak went unnoticed.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files.
findings.measuredBy: Glob "{src/**/*,test/**/*,tests/**/*}": only src/locks.js, src/worker.js, src/errors.js, src/payouts.js

findings.title: Plan inheritance now depends on case order and `// falls through` comments that get around the project's `no-fallthrough` lint rule
findings.scenario: Someone adds a new plan (for example 'business') between 'team' and 'free', or reorders the cases. Every plan above it then silently gains or loses features. Nothing about it looks wrong in review, because `// falls through` is exactly what tells `no-fallthrough` to stay quiet. Before this change, inheritance was written out in the data (`TEAM_FEATURES = [...FREE_FEATURES, ...]`), and an `ENTERPRISE_FEATURES = [...TEAM_FEATURES, 'sso', 'audit-log']` constant would have followed the existing pattern.
findings.whyNotPrevented: eslint.config.js sets 'no-fallthrough': 'error', but ESLint's default commentPattern accepts '// falls through', so lint passes. The tests sort their output and only check the three current plans.

findings.title: Refund sends money from the customer to the store instead of to the customer
findings.scenario: The signature is `transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents)` (src/ledger.js:9). Refunding a 5000-cent order to customer 'c1' calls transfer('store', 'c1', 5000). That lowers c1's balance by 5000 and raises the store's by 5000, so the customer is charged again. payouts.js:4 uses the correct order: transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, ...).
findings.whyNotPrevented: Both account ids are plain strings, so nothing in the types catches swapped arguments. The repo has no tests (Glob found only package.json and the src files). The to-before-from parameter order is easy to misread.

findings.title: Partial refunds can be repeated until they add up to more than the order total
findings.scenario: On an order with totalCents 1000, calling POST /refunds three times with amountCents 600 passes the check every time and refunds 1800 in total.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Each refund is checked only against order.totalCents. Nothing records how much has already been refunded, and neither the ledger nor the order keeps a refunded amount.

findings.title: The order, including its total and customer account, comes from the request body
findings.scenario: A caller can send any order, such as { totalCents: 999999, customerAccountId: 'attacker' }. The over-total check then compares against that made-up total, and the refund goes to whatever account the caller named. The route should look up the order by id on the server instead.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No order store or lookup exists, and no auth or role check is visible in routes.js. The existing /payouts route also trusts the body, so this follows the current pattern.

findings.title: Responses that arrive out of order replace newer results with older ones
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses past 200ms so a request for 'sho' starts, then types 'shoe'. If the 'sho' response arrives after the 'shoe' response, the list shows results for 'sho' while the input says 'shoe'. The same thing happens after a delete: the user deletes back to 's', the list is cleared to [], and then the in-flight 'sh' response fills it again.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The debounce only delays when a call starts. Nothing cancels an earlier fetch (no AbortController) or checks that `term` still matches `input.value` before calling renderResults. Firing a request on every pause makes overlapping requests normal, where the old submit-only flow rarely had them.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "AbortController|signal" in repo: no match; read src/debounce.js, which only clears the timer

findings.title: A failed search now becomes an unhandled promise rejection on every pause while typing
findings.scenario: When the API returns 500, searchProducts throws inside the async callback that the debounce timer calls. Nothing awaits or catches that promise, so each pause logs an unhandled rejection and the list keeps showing stale results.
findings.whyNotPrevented: api.js throws when the response is not ok, and debounce.js ignores what the callback returns. The submit handler had the same gap before, but it ran only on Enter.

findings.whyNotPrevented: The stated goal was to also search while typing. The diff adds a minimum length that applies to every search, and the submit handler no longer searches.

findings.title: Slow responses can arrive out of order and overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses past 200ms so a request starts, then types 'shoes'. If the 'sho' response comes back after the 'shoes' response, renderResults shows the results for 'sho' under the input 'shoes'. The same thing happens when the user deletes back to one character: the empty list renders right away, then the pending request for the older term fills the list again.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce.js only delays the call. It does not cancel requests already sent. search-box.js does not check that the term is still current before it renders, and api.js does not use an AbortController. Searching on every pause makes several requests in flight at once the normal case.

findings.title: A slow, older response can overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sh', waits 200ms (request A goes out), then types 'shoe' (request B goes out). If B returns first and A returns later, renderResults shows the 'sh' results while the box says 'shoe'. In the same way, after the user deletes back to one character and the list is cleared, a request still in flight fills it again with stale results.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce.js only delays when a call starts. Nothing cancels a request already in flight or checks that its term still matches input.value before rendering (Grep 'AbortController|signal' in repo: no match). There are no tests.

findings.title: Pressing Enter no longer searches; it only blocks the form submit
findings.scenario: The goal was to search while typing, not to stop Enter from working. Now Enter does nothing right away. Results come only when the pending debounce fires. If the input was filled without an 'input' event (for example set by script), Enter never searches at all.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The submit handler does not call the search function or flush the pending debounce.

findings.title: One-character searches are now impossible, even with Enter
findings.scenario: Before this change, a user could type 'a' and press Enter to get results. Now any term shorter than 2 characters clears the list and never calls the API.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The minimum length applies to every path because Enter shares the debounced handler. The author's goal does not mention this restriction.

findings.title: A failed search becomes an unhandled promise rejection on every pause
findings.scenario: When /api/products returns 500, searchProducts throws inside the setTimeout callback. The rejection is never caught, the old results stay on screen, and the user sees no error. This now happens on every pause while typing, not only when the user submits.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce.js discards the callback's return value, and nothing wraps the call in a try/catch.

finding.title: Saved preferences overwrite the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object and leak to other users

other.title: No tests for merging preferences or dropping unsupported keys

findings.title: Saved preferences overwrite the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object and leak to other users
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. GET /users/A writes theme='dark' into DEFAULT_PREFERENCES. User B has no saved preferences, but GET /users/B now returns theme:'dark'. The response bodies of every user also share one object, so later requests change earlier ones.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js:8 returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object itself (`return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;`), not a copy. Nothing freezes it, and package.json has no tests.

findings.title: `in` check accepts inherited keys like __proto__, constructor and toString as supported preferences
findings.scenario: Saved preferences JSON {"toString":"x","__proto__":{"admin":true}} goes through JSON.parse as own keys. `'toString' in preferences` is true, so the unsupported key gets copied into the response. Assigning `__proto__` replaces the prototype of the shared defaults object, so every user's preferences inherit `admin`. This goes against the goal of ignoring unsupported keys.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` walks the prototype chain. Only an own-key check on the defaults, like Object.hasOwn(defaults, key), would reject these keys, and no test covers it.

findings.title: No tests for merging preferences or dropping unsupported keys
findings.scenario: The two bugs above (the shared object getting mutated and inherited keys getting through) would pass unnoticed. No test checks that one user's preferences stay out of another user's response.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files and no test script.

findings.title: The `in` check accepts inherited keys like __proto__ and toString as supported preferences
findings.scenario: Saved preferences JSON {"toString":"x","__proto__":{"admin":true}} passes the `in` check because both keys exist on Object.prototype. toString ends up in the response even though it is not a supported key. The __proto__ assignment replaces the prototype of the preferences object, which is the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES. This breaks the goal of ignoring unsupported keys.

findings.title: The `in` check matches inherited keys, so retired or malicious keys like 'constructor' and '__proto__' get through
findings.scenario: A saved preferences_json of {"constructor":"x"} passes `'constructor' in preferences` because the key is inherited from Object.prototype. The response then includes preferences.constructor = 'x'. {"__proto__":{...}} from JSON.parse is an own key, so it also passes, and the assignment replaces the prototype of the shared defaults object.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` walks the prototype chain. An own-key check (Object.hasOwn) would block these keys, but none is used, and no test covers unsupported keys.
